Will Steam Machines solve Linux's gaming woes?

No, and frankly Betteridge would be proud of this clickbait headline.

The problem is that people who already understand Linux understand that it's cheaper to build your own machine. They understand that there's no advantage to buying a machine branded by Steam. They understand that there's far more to gain by customizing their favorite distro instead of using SteamOS. I can only assume that Steam Machine is supposed to be aimed at people who don't have the expertise to do this.

You have to try to see it from the perspective of the person who knows nothing: "Hey, buy our console. It only plays a subset of the games you currently play on your Windows PC and costs more. The games it does play sometimes have worse performance. You can't do anything else on it unless you know what you're doing. It ships with this powerful OS that has been intentionally limited so you don't blow off your own foot with a bazooka."

If it doesn't appeal to the power user and it doesn't appeal to the regular user, who's going to buy it?

I think Valve means well, but they need to come up with something that the Steam Machine does which becomes a "must have" function and/or feature. It needs to be marketed from a perspective that there is something tangible to gain by making a switch. Ironically, valve is actually competing with themselves in this regard. The only "killer feature" it has is streaming from a Windows PC to your television - however this is better served by the $50 Steam Link which I suspect will sell quite well due to it's low price point and specific functionality.

So far the success of Steam Machines all rest on a philosophical argument that only power users care about. "Doesn't need Windows!" will not be nearly enough to sway joe sixpack.
The steam machine seems more of an attempt to solve Valve's Microsoft woes, with the added benefit of getting some Linux customers.
